analysis.one_liner: Creates an independent federal board to investigate police killings, shootings, and severe use-of-force incidents.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote — it sat in two House committees from April 2021 until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a National Police Misuse of Force Investigation Board — an independent federal agency modeled on the aviation accident board — to investigate every death in police custody, officer-involved shooting, and use of force causing severe injury. Its findings would be admissible in court cases over police violence in states that take federal justice grants, and states that refused to cooperate could lose 1 to 10 percent of those grant funds. It would also give families of people killed or hurt by police a federal contact point and government-funded counseling. The bill was referred to two House committees, sent to subcommittees, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People injured or killed by police and their families: an independent board with subpoena power would investigate the incident, brief the family before any public briefing, and connect them to counseling services. Communities affected by police violence would gain public reports, demographic data on every investigated incident, and recommendations that governments must answer in writing within 90 days. In states taking Edward Byrne Memorial justice grants, board findings could be presented to juries in criminal and civil cases over police violence.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of police violence and their families

how_it_helps.text: Establishes an independent 8-member federal board, balanced between the parties, required to investigate deaths in police custody, officer-involved shootings, and uses of force causing severe bodily injury, with authority to compel witnesses and evidence by subpoena.

Requires states and localities receiving Byrne justice grants to make board findings and recommendations admissible in criminal or civil court over a police violence incident, including presenting them to a jury, and to report yearly on actions taken in response to board recommendations.

Lets the Justice Department cut 1 to 10 percent of a noncompliant state's or city's Byrne grant funds, with the money reallocated to complying states, and lets the Department's Civil Rights Division cite stalled recommendations as evidence in a pattern-or-practice investigation.

Requires the board to designate a family support director and an independent nonprofit to provide mental health and counseling services to civilians and families after a police killing or serious injury, and to brief families before any public briefing.
Makes board records available to the public and requires every recipient of a board recommendation to give a formal written response within 90 days, published alongside the recommendation.

analysis.who_pays: Police departments and their unions would face independent federal investigation of custody deaths, shootings, and severe force incidents, with findings usable against officers in court. State and local governments would take on new reporting duties and risk small cuts to their federal justice grants. Taxpayers would fund a new federal investigative agency authorized at 'such sums as may be necessary,' including at least one full-time investigator in states far from a regional office.
analysis.who_pays_short: Police departments, unions, and grant-receiving governments

drawbacks.text: The board's core product is recommendations, not enforcement: its only direct lever is a discretionary 1-to-10-percent reduction in Byrne grant funds, which departments and states could absorb, so most change would depend on DOJ follow-through.

Section 15 bars board reports from being admitted or used in civil lawsuits for damages, limiting families' ability to leverage board investigations in civil suits — in tension with Section 17's provision making board findings admissible in court.

The board would be funded by an open-ended appropriation ('such sums as may be necessary') for a permanent new federal agency with staff and investigative officers nationwide, a real recurring cost with no estimate attached.

The text carries over unadapted language from the aviation safety board it was modeled on, including an inquiry-member qualification rule about 'an aviation enterprise' and required evaluations of departments handling hazardous material transportation — signs of a repurposed template rather than police-specific drafting.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — independent federal investigation of deaths and shootings in police custody, with findings usable in court — addresses a real gap, since local investigations of police conduct are run by the same departments whose officers are involved. But the enforcement teeth are modest (a small, discretionary grant cut), the bill's own civil-lawsuit evidence bar undercuts families in the forum where most cases are actually litigated, and the open-ended funding of a new nationwide agency was never sized. A supporter would acknowledge the bill was an early, thinly drafted statement of principle rather than a finished oversight regime.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary and Transportation committees in April 2021, sent to subcommittees in each, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Ilhan Omar introduced the bill on April 28, 2021, joined by Rep. Eleanor Holmes Norton as the member who introduced it with her.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, the standard two-committee split the Speaker uses for bills spanning jurisdictions.

On April 29, 2021 it was referred to the Transportation Committee's Economic Development, Public Buildings, and Emergency Management Subcommittee, and on October 19, 2021 to the Judiciary Committee's Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security Subcommittee.
No further action of any kind — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.
The bill attracted 6 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican support at any point.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police departments and their unions are better off: no independent federal board will investigate custody deaths, shootings, or severe force incidents, and internal department reviews remain the primary mechanism. State and local governments also gain, keeping full control of use-of-force investigations and their Byrne grant funds without new reporting duties.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police departments and unions avoiding independent oversight

sides.party_line_note: All seven supporters — the sponsor and 6 cosponsors — were Democrats, and no vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; the bill died with purely Democratic sponsorship and no Republican backing.

industries.note: The bill would strip departments of sole control over investigating officer-involved deaths and shootings, handing custody-death and shooting cases to an independent federal board with subpoena power, and make board findings usable against officers in court. Union opposition to federal use-of-force oversight was a central obstacle to police accountability legislation in this Congress.

industries.industry: State and local governments receiving federal justice grants
industries.note: Governments would take on yearly reporting duties and risk a 1-to-10-percent cut to Byrne grant funds for noncompliance, though complying governments keep their money and gain court-admissible investigative findings. Their institutional interest in avoiding conditions on federal funds runs against the accountability the bill would create.
The bill would designate an independent nonprofit for each investigated incident to coordinate mental health care and support for victims and families, a funded coordinating role for the sector.
